sections.h2: Which office handles an Odessa tax account?
sections.html:
One Odessa account can fund many units at once, and the Ector County Appraisal District is the first office to call. The Texas Comptroller's county directory lists the City of Odessa, Ector County, Ector County ISD, the Odessa Junior College District, a county hospital district, a utility district and two emergency service districts among the active taxing units.

The same directory says the Ector County tax assessor-collector's office does not collect property tax, and that in a county like that the appraisal district may be the collector. The appraisal district's own site describes its job as appraisal and tax collection, and it publishes 432-332-6834 for questions about amounts due. Its office is at 1301 E. 8th St. in Odessa.

Some Odessa addresses fall in Midland County. The city's budget FAQ states that the city does not set values, and that the Ector County or Midland County appraisal district does, depending on where the property sits. Confirm which district holds your parcel before you look up an account or file a protest.

sections.h2: What is the Odessa city property tax rate?
sections.html:
The city's 2026-27 taxpayer impact statement lists $0.471578 per $100 of valuation for the city's share of the bill. The prior year's rate on the same page is $0.470700. The city's FAQ says it spends property tax on firefighters, police officers, road repairs and parks.

The city's slice is small next to the whole account, since the school district, county, college, hospital district and any special district each add a rate of their own.

Odessa's FAQ compares the city with its neighbors. It lists Midland's proposed 2026-27 rate at $0.383092, Lubbock's at $0.482106 and Abilene's at $0.7496. It also reports average home appraisals of $201,754 in Odessa and $402,171 in Midland, which is why Midland collects more gross tax revenue ($62.1 million against about $46.0 million for Odessa) at a lower rate.

Property tax supplies 15.8 percent of the city's revenue, and sales tax supplies 18.2 percent. The city's piece of sales tax is 1.25 percent of the 8.25 percent total.

sections.h2: When is Odessa property tax due, and what does a late payment cost?
sections.html:
Treat January 31 as a cliff. Statements arrive in the fall, and the account stays clean through the end of January. On February 1 the collector starts adding charges, and the balance keeps swelling through the summer.

  • First of February: six percent goes on as a penalty and one percent as interest.
  • Every month afterward: another point of penalty, so the penalty hits 12 percent when July begins. Interest never stops at one percent per month.
  • A taxing unit that has a delinquent-tax lawyer under contract may tack on as much as one fifth of the balance.
  • Paying in halves is allowed: the first by the end of November, the second by the end of June.

Older or disabled homestead owners have a four-payment path. Any homestead owner already behind may request a longer plan, and some collectors stretch it to 36 months. A request to forgive penalty and interest needs the tax paid within three weeks of learning about the problem, and the written request must go in before day 181.

sections.h2: How can an Odessa homeowner lower the tax bill?
sections.html:
Begin with the homestead exemption, then read the appraisal notice each spring. The appraisal district posts a 2026 sheet titled Exemption Amounts by Entity, which shows what every Odessa-area unit gives, including the city, the county and the college.

  • School tax: the first $140,000 of a homestead's value is exempt.
  • Seniors and disabled owners: a further $60,000 is shielded from school tax. Claiming the senior break drops the disabled one.
  • Optional breaks: a unit may pick a percentage of up to 20 percent, never below $5,000.
  • Growth limit: once a homestead exemption is in place, the appraised value may rise only 10 percent annually.
  • Freeze: seniors and disabled owners generally lock the school levy at the first qualifying year's amount.

Applications go to the appraisal district before May 1. Buyers who close after New Year's Day can still claim for the remainder of that year if the previous owner never did. Disabled veterans get a sliding exemption tied to their VA rating that tops out at $12,000, and a veteran rated 100 percent pays no tax on the residence homestead.

Protests are due on May 15, or 30 days after you receive the notice if that falls later. An owner still unhappy after the review board hearing can sue in district court, ask for binding arbitration, or go before the State Office of Administrative Hearings when the disputed value tops $1,000,000.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid Odessa property tax when the house is sold?
sections.html:
The lien is born on January 1 and goes wherever the house goes. A buyer cannot receive clear title while delinquent amounts remain, and whoever owned on that January 1 can still be pursued for the year's bill. Expect the title company to prorate the current year on the settlement sheet.

When delinquent tax ends in a tax foreclosure sale, a former homestead owner gets two years after the buyer's deed is filed to buy it back, and other property gets 180 days. The buy-back price carries a premium over the bid. Leftover sale money can be claimed by the prior owner, but only for a 24-month window.

Odessa adds a few city rules a seller meets before listing. Residential building permits come from the Building Inspection division at 411 W. 8th Street, by phone at 432-335-3214 or through the online portal. If the city engineer calls a sidewalk, driveway or curb hazardous, the adjoining owner has 30 days from notice to fix it. Owners of rentals must keep working smoke detectors in each unit.

sections.h2: What do Census figures show about Odessa housing?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau measures Odessa at 51.08 square miles of land and 2,240 residents per square mile in 2020. Headcount moved from 99,940 in 2010 to 114,428 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate of 122,707 sits 7.2 percent above the 2020 base.

Survey data for 2020-2024 shows 46,660 households and an ownership rate of 59.8 percent. The middle owner-occupied home is valued at $223,100, with monthly owner costs of $1,924 for those carrying a mortgage. Renters pay $1,315 at the median, while household income at the median is $73,472, and workers travel 22.4 minutes each way. Those are midpoints for the whole city, so one street can differ, and your own appraisal sets your own bill.

faqs.q: Is Odessa property tax due on January 31?
faqs.a: Yes, January 31 is the last clean day. On February 1 the balance turns delinquent and charges begin, and by July the penalty alone has grown to 12 percent.

faqs.q: Where does an Odessa owner send the tax payment?
faqs.a: Call the Ector County Appraisal District at 432-332-6834 first. The Comptroller's directory says the county's assessor-collector office does not collect, and the appraisal district may. A parcel in Midland County follows that county's appraisal district.

faqs.q: What is the Odessa city tax rate for 2026-27?
faqs.a: The city's own statement lists $0.471578 for every $100 of valuation. School, county, college and special-district rates come on top of it.

faqs.q: Does Odessa have its own homestead exemption?
faqs.a: Request the appraisal district's 2026 Exemption Amounts by Entity sheet, which names the amount each unit grants, the City of Odessa included. State law fixes only the school district break at $140,000, and any other unit may adopt an optional percentage exemption.

faqs.q: What if I sell an Odessa house that owes back taxes?
faqs.a: Back tax is usually paid out of the sale money at the closing table, because the lien rides with the lot. No buyer gets clean title before that happens, and the January 1 owner stays on the hook for that year's tax.
